Hello folks,

I've already got my hand dirty in Linux some time ago (debian and ubuntu mainly), and with all the mess I keep reading here and there about Microsoft's freemium Win10, I'm seriously considering switching to Linux for gaming. But I've heard also that gaming on Linux could get difficult sometimes (poor GPU drivers support, bad ports, less coverage...).

On the other side, with Win10 comes DX12, which seems to bring a second life to my aging GPU and CPU. And the choice of games. And the frequent updates. Well, all the advantages of running 90% of the world's computers, I guess.

So what could convince people to switch to Linux for gaming and why ?
Win10 incoming, I'm considering switching to Linux for gaming, but...

As I see it Linux isn't built of gaming. It can game and the support for it on steam has been great, but with Microsoft and Apple completely dominating the market, there is a higher demand for games to be compatible with those systems compared to Linux. There are some good Linux gaming distros (Steam OS and Play Linux) but in the end they are still Linux which get unfairly pushed to the side to be dealt with later.

A few thoughts:

Game Selection: The selection of games that run natively (that is, that aren't being run through some form of emulation or abstraction. e.g.: wine, crossover, virtual machine, etc) is smaller than what's available on Windows - this is not a surprise to anyone right now. The number is growing quite rapidly. Looking right now on Steam at the Top Sellers 3 of the top 10 have a linux-native version available right now, and at least two others have one in the works. Of the top 25, 8 have linux-native versions (and about 5 more have one in the works). Those results will, of course, change a bit depending on your filters and when you check, but that's about right on average.

That may not seem like much, but this number, by comparison, was a big ol' zero just about two-odd years ago. Valve has made a HUGE push to get vendors to support linux as part of their Steam Machine initiative, so these numbers have been trending very favorably in the last few years. If you add wine to the equation, that unlocks nearly all of the top 25, though some do require a little bit of effort to get working. Tools like Code Weaver's Crossover product can make setup much easier, but can have some limitations of their own.

One other issue that should be noted is genre. Some genres of games are definitely better supported (natively) than others. If you're looking for a good, triple-AAA MMORPG for example, don't hold your breath (or start looking at wine).

GPU support: This is a real factor for some people. This is just a high level summary, of course, but... - Intel: Some of the best, most complete open source support, but also the weakest in terms of firepower being brought to the table. I mention them if only because, well, heck, they're trying. :)
- nVidia: The open source drivers are often in a state of playing "catch up", but the closed-drivers from nVidia are solid and complete (but closed-source which is a real problem for some folks).
- AMD: Better open source support, but generally a worse product. Many people seem to have a lot of problems with AMD drivers and games on linux.
I'm glossing over the details, obviously, but the key take away you should have is: nVidia. Just use nVidia and you'll be fine. You're not completely screwed if you use something else, but you'll be making things harder for yourself.

Port Quality: What constitutes a "good" port for many users (not all; i don't speak for everyone) really seems to come down to whether or not they used a common video card and up-to-date drivers. This is actually a problem for windows users too, but - see above - AMD users seem to have a hard time. This doesn't mean all ports are perfect - even with great hardware - but the truly terrible ports are relatively rare and can be sussed out quickly with a look at the reviews. Will you never see a problem? No. But it's not as bad as it may seem at first glance. I suspect part of the reputation for "bad ports" is more a matter of the nature of user-based reporting - one will rarely need to post that everything-is-fine, but you can bet that if people do have a problem, it'll be mentioned and mentioned often. Take a look at any video-game subforum here (or on reddit) - how many posts are from people saying that they installed and played just fine? How many are from people that had a problem?

Win10/DX12 - some others have already made some good comments re: DX12 vs 11 vs 10, etc - i won't rehash that (i'm rambling as it is). I will point out that, from a "get more life out of your computer" factor, most linux distros are going to beat Windows hands-down. Win10 is quite demanding in terms of hardware needs compared to linux. Windows also has some more "philosophical" issues that some users find quickly tips the balance for them (privacy, security, etc) - but you didn't ask about that, so I won't go into it.

So should you make the switch? Eh. Up to you. The world's not going to end if you pick one OS over the other. :) I would suggest that you do three things:
1) Review you hardware, in particular, your video card. Don't trust one or three random guys on the internet, but do a bit of real digging and see what kind of driver support you'll have and what issues others have seen.
2) Look at your top ten or top twenty game list. Now look on Steam, Wine's add database and other tools (https://www.codeweavers.com/, https://www.playonlinux.com, etc) and see what games work, work-with-effort, and don't-work-at-all.
3) Test drive. If you haven't played with a recent edition of Debian, Ubuntu, etc, go check out the recent versions. Download and install into a virtual machine or on a live-cd/live-USB install. It may turn out that you positively loathe the current state of things on the linux desktop, in which case, this is all moot. But the point is: explore the current options and go in with all of the information.
